title: What Actually Backs the Value of Money?
question: A dollar isn't backed by gold anymore, and it isn't intrinsically useful the way food or tools are — so what makes it worth anything at all?
summary: Money's value turns out to rest neither on a commodity nor on government decree alone, but on a self-sustaining web of mutual expectation, enforced by taxation and habit — a fiction so stable that most people never notice it's a fiction.
content:
The barter myth, debunked

The textbook story is that money emerged to solve the "double coincidence of wants" problem in barter economies — I have wheat, you have shoes, but you don't want wheat, so we needed a universal medium of exchange. Anthropologists who actually studied pre-monetary societies, notably David Graeber, found almost no historical evidence that barter economies of this kind ever existed at scale. What existed instead were elaborate systems of credit, obligation, and communal reciprocity: you gave your neighbor a goat because you'd eventually need something from them, and everyone kept rough informal track. Money, on this view, didn't replace barter — it formalized and depersonalized preexisting credit relationships, letting debts be settled with strangers rather than only within a web of ongoing social trust.

Three competing theories of what backs it

Commodity theory says money is valuable because it represents or is convertible into something intrinsically valuable, like gold — this was the world of the gold standard, abandoned by the US in 1971. Chartalism (state theory of money) says money's value comes from the state's willingness to accept it, and only it, in payment of taxes; since everyone in the jurisdiction owes taxes, everyone needs the currency, which manufactures demand for otherwise worthless paper. Credit theory treats money as a generalized IOU — a token representing a claim on future goods or labor, with the issuer's credibility as collateral. Modern fiat currencies like the dollar are best explained by a blend of chartalism and credit theory: no gold backs them, but the government's taxing power and the central bank's credibility do.

The self-fulfilling prophecy problem

Here's the strange part: even chartalism doesn't fully explain why money is accepted between two people who owe no taxes to anyone, such as in international trade or black markets. The deepest layer of the answer is coordination: a dollar is valuable to me because I believe others will accept it from me later, and they believe the same about others, recursively, with no bottom. This is a coordination equilibrium, similar in structure to why everyone drives on the same side of the road — no individual reason is required beyond "everyone else does it." Game theorists call situations like this a Nash equilibrium in beliefs: it's self-sustaining precisely because deviating unilaterally (refusing to accept money) makes you worse off, not better, even though the underlying convention is arbitrary.

What breaks the illusion

Hyperinflation episodes are the clearest natural experiments showing money's value is a fragile social agreement rather than an intrinsic property. In Weimar Germany and Zimbabwe, the physical currency didn't change, the laws often didn't change quickly, but the belief that others would keep accepting the currency tomorrow collapsed, and with it the currency's usefulness collapsed too — sometimes within weeks. Cryptocurrencies are an interesting modern test case from the opposite direction: they have no state backing and no tax-driven demand, yet some sustain real value purely through decentralized, voluntary coordination on scarcity and shared belief, suggesting that state enforcement, while historically dominant, may not be strictly necessary for a monetary equilibrium to hold — just very effective at stabilizing one.

perspectives.title: Anthropological Perspective
perspectives.description: Historical evidence undermines the standard barter-origin story; money more plausibly formalized preexisting communal credit and obligation systems rather than solving a barter coordination problem that rarely existed in practice.

perspectives.title: Economic Perspective
perspectives.description: Chartalism explains fiat currency's baseline demand through mandatory tax obligations, while credit theory frames money as a transferable IOU whose value depends on the issuer's perceived reliability.

perspectives.title: Game-Theoretic Perspective
perspectives.description: Money's acceptance is a self-reinforcing coordination equilibrium: it's rational to accept currency only because you expect others will too, with no need for any deeper, non-circular justification.

perspectives.title: Historical Perspective
perspectives.description: Hyperinflation events reveal money's value as socially contingent rather than intrinsic — the physical tokens and legal structures can remain unchanged while collective belief in future acceptance collapses, destroying the currency's function within weeks.

perspectives.title: Technological Perspective
perspectives.description: Cryptocurrencies test whether state enforcement is necessary for monetary equilibria, showing that decentralized coordination on scarcity and shared belief can sustain value without a taxing authority, though usually with far more volatility.

connections: David Graeber's 'Debt: The First 5,000 Years' and the barter myth

Nash equilibria and focal points in coordination games
Hyperinflation in Weimar Germany and Zimbabwe
The social construction of institutional facts (Searle's 'status functions')
openQuestions: If money's value is fundamentally a coordination equilibrium, why does state backing so consistently produce more stable currencies than purely voluntary schemes?
Could a currency with no state backing and no scarcity mechanism ever sustain long-term value purely through social convention?
How much of modern economic instability traces back to the fact that money's foundation is belief rather than anything physically fixed?
Is there a meaningful difference between money's 'fictional' value and other institutional facts like citizenship or corporate personhood, or are they all the same phenomenon?
